name: Celtuce
summary: Celtuce is a stem-lettuce crop type within Lactuca sativa, grown mainly for its enlarged edible stalk and also for its leaves. Long photoperiods can trigger premature bolting; the stalk then elongates and the crop can become bitter before harvest. No named cultivar or home-system prescription is represented.

identity.guidance: UC Davis and NC State use Celtuce for stem lettuce within Lactuca sativa. POWO recognizes the species; the crop-group name does not establish a separate species or cultivar.

growth.short: Leafy top with an enlarged, tender edible stem
growth.guidance: UC Davis and UC Cooperative Extension distinguish celtuce by its enlarged edible stem, with leaves also used as food. Stem size varies with the selected line and harvest stage; no fixed mature dimensions are assigned to this crop group.

cultivation.short: Long photoperiods can shorten the useful stem-growing season
cultivation.guidance: UC Davis reports that long photoperiods promote premature bolting in celtuce, while UC Cooperative Extension describes intense sun as a regional bolting pressure in the Central Sierra and suggests partial sun or shade cloth there. Treat this as outdoor seasonal context, not an indoor-light prescription. Crop-specific spacing, a universal calendar and hydroponic compatibility remain unestablished.

harvestUse.short: The tender stem is primary; leaves are also edible
harvestUse.guidance: Harvest use centers on the thick stem; UC Davis describes it as the primary edible product and reports both raw and cooked use, while UC Cooperative Extension also identifies the leaves as edible. Long-day bolting can make the crop bitter before the stem is harvested. No universal stalk size or maturity day is assigned.

flowering.short: Long days can trigger premature stem elongation
flowering.guidance: UC Davis describes celtuce as day-length-sensitive: long photoperiods can induce bolting, an early transition to flowering in which the stem elongates. This is a developmental response, not a target for edible-stem production.

problems.short: Premature bolting can make the crop bitter before harvest
problems.guidance: UC Davis reports that long days can cause celtuce to bolt and become bitter before the edible stem is harvested, shortening the useful season. UC Cooperative Extension describes intense sun as a local bolting pressure in the Central Sierra; that regional note is not a universal calendar or an indoor-light response.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: No cited source evaluates this crop type in a hydroponic system.

evidence.note: Lettuce crop type selected for an enlarged stem.

height.reason: No comparable mature dimension is established for the crop group.

spread.reason: No comparable mature dimension is established for the crop group.

spacing.reason: No spacing recommendation is assigned from the selected crop-group sources.

light.reason: Outdoor photoperiod and exposure guidance is not translated into indoor grow-light intensity.

name: Flax
summary: An annual species grown for either stem fiber or seed/oil. Those production types differ in stature, branching, stand density, harvest stage, and processing; this species-level identity does not specify a cultivar or promise a dual-purpose crop.

identity.short: Accepted species; fiber flax and linseed are production types
identity.guidance: POWO accepts Linum usitatissimum. North Dakota State and Wisconsin Extension distinguish fiber flax from seed/oil flax within this species; the present identity does not identify a variety or intended crop use.

growth.short: Annual, upright crop; height and branching vary with production type
growth.guidance: NDSU describes an annual plant with a main stem, usually 24–36 inches in its North Dakota field context. Fiber varieties are generally taller and less branched; seed types are shorter and more branched. Wisconsin Extension likewise reports around three feet but stresses type and stand-density differences. These field-crop descriptions do not establish a garden or container dimension for an unspecified seed lot.

cultivation.short: Full sun and well-drained soil; select guidance for the intended flax type
cultivation.guidance: NC State Extension describes common flax as best in full sun and as preferring moist, well-drained soil; it also notes drought tolerance, not a reason to keep the crop dry. Wisconsin's early-spring timing, stand density, and seeding-rate guidance is regional field production and differs substantially between fiber and seed flax. Do not translate those rates into home-container spacing or infer hydroponic suitability.

propagation.short: Annual crop propagated by seed; this is not a seed-starting protocol
propagation.guidance: NC State Extension lists seed propagation for common flax, and crop references describe field establishment from seed. This confirms the propagation mode only; sowing depth, temperature, and seedling care belong in a supported Seed Profile or locally appropriate protocol and are not specified here.

harvestUse.short: Fiber and seed crops are harvested at different stages
harvestUse.guidance: Wisconsin Extension reports fiber flax harvested before seed maturity, commonly around 90–100 days after sowing, while seed flax may take around 90–120 days depending on variety and conditions. NDSU's North Dakota field guide gives a seed-harvest cue: about 90% of bolls brown, even if stems remain green. These are regional crop-production references, not a universal home-garden calendar. Fiber is traditionally pulled and then requires retting and further processing; flaxseed is also used whole or ground in foods, while the oil is suited to dressings/sauces rather than high-heat cooking. NC State flags large-quantity ingestion/contact irritation; no intake amount, home-storage duration, or processing safety rule is inferred here.

flowering.short: Pale-blue flowers appear over a crop flowering period
flowering.guidance: NC State describes pale-blue flowers on slender stems from late spring into mid-summer in its regional plant profile. Wisconsin notes that an individual flower lasts one day; NDSU describes an approximately 25-day flowering phase in field production, which can extend under favorable moisture. Timing varies with region and crop type; this is not a fixed bloom date.

problems.short: Scout for occasional cutworms and grasshoppers; no resistance is claimed
problems.guidance: NC State lists cutworms and grasshoppers as occasional pests. Wisconsin Extension identifies early weed competition and fungal disease management as field-production concerns, including rotation to help control Fusarium rust and other fungi. NC State also flags large-quantity ingestion and contact irritation; because crop sources discuss food uses but do not provide a safety threshold here, this profile makes no consumption-dose or processing claim. No cultivar resistance is asserted. NDSU lists several field diseases and insect risks, but its variety-specific resistance table is not applied to this unspecified identity.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: The selected evidence concerns outdoor soil and field production; it does not establish hydroponic suitability.

evidence.note: Annual field crop form; fiber versus seed type and cultivar are unspecified.

height.reason: Field sources report about 24–36 inches but also document substantial fiber/seed type differences; no single dimension is assigned to the unspecified identity.

spread.reason: No garden-scale spread is established; stand density is not plant spread or pod spacing.

spacing.reason: Agricultural stand densities differ by fiber or seed purpose and are not converted into home or pod spacing.

light.reason: Full-sun outdoor guidance does not define an indoor grow-light intensity category.

name: Rice
summary: Cultivated rice at species level, with materially different flooded lowland and upland production systems. The crop lifecycle is documented, and a UF/IFAS county-extension home trial describes two named types in a small pot. It is not a universal cultivar-specific container protocol or household grain-yield estimate.

identity.short: Accepted cultivated rice species; subspecies and cultivar not assigned
identity.guidance: POWO accepts Oryza sativa. Rice cultivars and subspecies vary; this identity does not assign japonica, indica, grain type, or a named cultivar without seed-lot evidence.

growth.short: Annual cereal progressing through vegetative, reproductive and grain-ripening stages
growth.guidance: The Arkansas Rice Production Handbook organizes development as vegetative growth, reproductive development and maturation/ripening. USDA describes both flooded and non-flooded production systems. These are crop-scale references; cultivar, climate and water regime affect timing and plant dimensions, which are not assigned.

care.short: One UF/IFAS backyard pot-and-tray setup is experimental, not universal
care.guidance: UF/IFAS Charlotte County Extension describes a small-scale experiment using an 8-inch pot with a water tray, maintaining about 1–1.5 inches of water in the tray during the growing season. Its author names Blue Bonnet as upland rice and Carolina Gold as a wet type, and explicitly frames the method as experimental. Keep this as one regional home-garden example, not a prescription for an unidentified cultivar. The article suggests a screened location to deter mosquitoes around standing water. This soil-and-tray method does not establish recirculating hydroponic suitability.

cultivation.short: Water management depends on production system; flooded culture is not universal
cultivation.guidance: USDA documents multiple commercial production systems. NC State Extension distinguishes upland rice from standing-water production: it is grown more like other grain crops, with irrigation at critical stages such as pollination. This regional field example demonstrates that flooding is not universal. A separate UF/IFAS county-extension educator describes an explicitly experimental backyard setup with named upland and wet-type varieties; it is practical context, not a universal recipe for an unidentified rice type or evidence of hydroponic suitability.

propagation.short: Seed-grown; sowing protocol belongs in Seed Profile
propagation.guidance: Rice production uses grain seed. This Plant Profile records the propagation mode only; seed-lot viability, sowing depth, temperature and germination protocol belong in Seed Profile and are not inferred for an unidentified lot.

harvestUse.short: Harvest follows grain maturation; field drying and milling remain system-dependent
harvestUse.guidance: The harvested crop is mature grain. The Arkansas handbook treats maturity, harvest, drying and milling as production-system steps; those field/commercial procedures do not establish a household harvest date, drying method, milling result, or cultivar-specific use for this identity.

flowering.short: Pollination is a critical reproductive stage, including for upland rice
flowering.guidance: NC State Extension identifies pollination as a critical irrigation stage for the upland rice crop it describes. This supports the importance of reproductive-stage water management in that regional field system, not a universal watering schedule or a cultivar-specific flowering date.

problems.short: Recognize sheath lesions as a regional field-disease warning, not a diagnosis by itself
problems.guidance: The Arkansas handbook describes rice sheath blight as lesions on sheaths/leaves that can spread vertically under hot, humid field conditions. This is a commercial Arkansas disease reference; similar-looking lesions need diagnosis, and the source does not justify a cultivar-resistance claim or household pesticide recommendation.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: Field rice production, including standing-water culture, does not establish compatibility with recirculating hydroponics.

evidence.note: Annual cereal grass; subspecies and variety unspecified.

height.reason: No cultivar-specific home-growing dimension is provided.

spread.reason: No household spacing or spread is provided.

spacing.reason: Agricultural seeding rates are not mapped to home or pod spacing.

light.reason: No indoor grow-light requirement is established.

name: Spring Barley
summary: Cool-season annual barley sown in spring; spring type does not require winter vernalization. Minnesota field evidence documents tillering, pollination and grain maturity, while Extension sources add home-relevant light, soil and grain-handling context without identifying a cultivar, food-grade seed lot, or indoor/system fit.

identity.short: Accepted species Hordeum vulgare; spring is a crop type, not a cultivar
identity.guidance: POWO accepts Hordeum vulgare. UMN distinguishes spring barley, which can be sown in spring without winter vernalization, from winter barley that requires cold exposure. This record represents the spring-sown type and does not assign a named cultivar, two-row/six-row form, malting quality or end use.

growth.short: Tillers form over weeks; some natural tiller loss is part of development
growth.guidance: In UMN's Minnesota spring-barley field context, tillers emerge over roughly a two-week span and their number varies with variety and conditions. Some tillers normally die without forming a head about four weeks after crop emergence. This can be normal development; greater premature tiller death or fewer tillers under poor/stressed conditions is a warning to assess growing conditions, not a standalone diagnosis. NC State's species-level garden profile gives a broad 1–4 ft height and 6–12 in width range; these landscape dimensions are not a prediction for an unspecified spring crop cultivar or an indoor container.

cultivation.short: Full sun and well-drained soil; keep field guidance distinct from indoor growing
cultivation.guidance: NC State Extension describes Hordeum vulgare as a full-sun species adaptable to several soil types if drainage is good; its gardening account favors moderately fertile ground not subject to flooding. This provides outdoor species-level context, not indoor grow-light requirements or a container recipe. UMN reports pollination near head emergence, about six to seven weeks after emergence in its Minnesota field guide; high temperature or water deficit during pollen formation can reduce kernel number. That stage timing is regional, not a guaranteed calendar. Field germination temperature and coleoptile planting depth belong to seed establishment, not mature-plant care.

propagation.short: Grain-seed propagation; detailed sowing belongs in seed guidance
propagation.guidance: Spring barley is raised from grain seed. This Plant Profile records the propagation mode only; UMN's minimum germination temperature and field sowing depth are establishment facts and are not repeated as mature-plant care. No named cultivar or household seed-starting protocol is represented here.

harvestUse.short: Hard kernels and loss of green indicate maturity; harvest use depends on the lot
harvestUse.guidance: UMN identifies hard dough as the stage when kernels become firmer and lose green color; loss of green from glumes and peduncle indicates physiological maturity in its field context. NCSU lists barley for grain and as a source of flour or malt. UC ANR describes cutting and bundling fully ripe small-grain stalks, then threshing and winnowing at home. These sources do not identify this seed lot as food-grade or malting quality; UMN's 13–14% moisture combine threshold is not a household storage instruction.

flowering.short: Pollination occurs near head emergence and is stress-sensitive
flowering.guidance: UMN's Minnesota guide places pollination just before or during head emergence, approximately six to seven weeks after crop emergence. It notes that water deficit or high temperature during pollen formation can reduce kernel number. Timing varies by cultivar and conditions; do not treat the regional estimate as a universal date.

problems.short: Distinguish expected tiller dieback from excessive loss under stress
problems.guidance: Some spring-barley tillers naturally die without producing a head. UMN says poor or stressed growing conditions can result in fewer tillers or more premature tiller death; the pattern is a prompt to review conditions, not enough to identify a specific disease or nutrient deficiency. No resistance or pesticide claim is made.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: Field cereal guidance does not establish hydroponic suitability.

evidence.note: Spring-sown Hordeum vulgare crop type; cultivar unspecified.

height.reason: No home-scale cultivar dimension is supplied.

spread.reason: No household spacing or spread is supplied.

spacing.reason: Field seeding-rate recommendations are not container spacing.

light.reason: No indoor light requirement is established.

name: Grain Sorghum
summary: A warm-season grain crop within Sorghum bicolor. Its stages and maturity depend on hybrid and conditions; grain sorghum is kept distinct from forage types, and field guidance is not a container or hydroponic recipe.

identity.short: Sorghum bicolor; grain-crop type, no cultivar assigned
identity.guidance: POWO accepts Sorghum bicolor. NC State distinguishes grain sorghum used for food from grass sorghum grown for feed. This profile represents the grain type only; no cultivar, hybrid, or food-processing method is assigned.

growth.short: Warm-season annual grass with cultivar-dependent stages and size
growth.guidance: USDA and Texas A&M describe sorghum as a warm-season grain crop. Growth proceeds through vegetative, panicle-development, and grain-fill stages; hybrid maturity and conditions affect timing. Plant height varies by cultivar and production purpose, so no single mature dimension is assigned.

cultivation.short: Protect panicle development and flowering from severe water stress
cultivation.guidance: Texas A&M reports that severe drought at boot/panicle exertion can reduce flowering and seed set, and that the crop is especially sensitive to stress around this stage. Its guidance is field-scale and Texas-scoped; OSU's soil-temperature and planting-depth recommendations are regional field instructions, not a home-container schedule. Do not infer hydroponic suitability or a universal watering interval.

propagation.short: Seed-sown grain crop; household protocol is not established here
propagation.guidance: Grain sorghum is propagated from seed. OSU documents field sowing for Eastern Oregon, but field rates and depths are not converted to container instructions; no cultivar-specific household seed-starting protocol is claimed in this Plant Profile.

harvestUse.short: Harvest mature grain; food/feed use depends on the represented type and lot
harvestUse.guidance: The identity is grain sorghum, not forage biomass. NC State describes grain sorghum as a food crop and distinguishes grass sorghum used for feed; the named profile does not establish a specific hybrid, processing method, or food/feed grade. Texas A&M identifies a black layer near the kernel base as physiological maturity; commercial moisture thresholds are not household storage instructions.

flowering.short: Panicle emergence and flowering precede grain fill
flowering.guidance: Texas A&M's grain-sorghum guide reports yellow anthers beginning to appear about 5–7 days after panicle exertion, with flowering progressing down the panicle. The timing is hybrid- and condition-dependent, not a calendar promise. Severe drought at boot can impair panicle exertion and seed set.

problems.short: Scout panicles for midge/headworms and grain for bird damage
problems.guidance: Texas A&M lists sorghum midge damage to developing seed and advises examining leaves for greenbugs and panicles for headworms; its midge note is scoped to central and south Texas. OSU identifies bird feeding as a field-crop risk around soft dough and lists regional insect and disease concerns. At hard dough, drought, disease or stalk-borer injury can contribute to lodging. These are recognition cues, not a cultivar-resistance claim or pesticide recommendation.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: Field production sources do not evaluate this crop in hydroponics.

evidence.note: Warm-season grain crop; forage hybrids excluded.

height.reason: Cultivar and production purpose are unspecified.

spacing.reason: Field seeding rates do not define pod or container spacing.

light.reason: No indoor grow-light requirement is established.

name: Proso Millet
summary: A warm-season annual grass grown for its short-season grain. The profile distinguishes cultivated proso millet from foxtail, pearl and wild-proso forms; cultivar and household-scale performance are not specified.

identity.guidance: POWO accepts Panicum miliaceum as proso/common millet. “Millet” also names other crop species, including foxtail and pearl millet, which are not represented here.

growth.short: Warm-season annual grass with an open grain panicle
growth.guidance: USDA describes a short-season crop that commonly matures in about 60–90 days after planting; University of Wisconsin’s Minnesota/Wisconsin field context reports about 70–90 days depending on variety. The latter describes proso at roughly 40 inches tall. These are crop/region observations, not a guaranteed home-crop calendar or cultivar dimension. The flowering period is brief.

cultivation.short: Warm, frost-sensitive crop; full sun and well-drained soil
cultivation.guidance: USDA reports best growth in full sun and a broad moist-to-dry range, but also notes that shallow roots limit performance under water stress and the crop is not frost tolerant. UW–Madison’s regional field guide describes well-drained loam as suitable and waterlogged soil as unsuitable. Read these as field-crop context: drought tolerance does not mean keep a container dry, and field seeding rates are not home spacing or hydroponic guidance.

propagation.short: Seed-grown crop; no dedicated Seed Profile is published
propagation.guidance: Cultivated proso millet is raised from seed. This Plant Profile records the propagation mode only; no dedicated Seed Profile is currently published for this identity. USDA field drilling rates and row spacing are not converted into household sowing instructions or pod spacing.

flowering.short: A brief flowering phase precedes grain fill
flowering.guidance: The USDA plant guide describes a short, roughly one-week flowering period for the crop. It does not establish a repeat-flowering or ornamental-bloom expectation for a home-grown plant.

harvestUse.short: Watch the panicle for uneven ripening and shattering
harvestUse.guidance: USDA gives a broad 60–90-day crop maturity range. In the Minnesota/Wisconsin field guide, harvest readiness begins when seeds in the upper half of the panicle are mature and lower seeds have lost their green color, even if stems remain green. Seeds mature from the top downward and can shatter, so waiting for every stem to brown can lose grain; field harvest methods are not a household threshing or storage protocol. USDA documents the species as a human-food grain in several regions and as birdseed/feed in the United States, but does not establish processing instructions for an unidentified seed lot.

problems.short: Avoid frost, waterlogging and delayed grain harvest
problems.guidance: The crop is frost-sensitive; waterlogged soil is unsuitable, while shallow roots mean prolonged water stress can still reduce growth despite the species’ relative drought tolerance. USDA reports occasional grasshopper, thrips and European corn borer feeding, and warns that escaped wild-proso forms can become weedy; do not treat those observations as a cultivar-specific resistance profile. USDA’s 2026 state seed-rule compilation for Colorado separately list wild-proso millet (Panicum miliaceum subsp. ruderale); check local rules and use correctly identified cultivated grain seed rather than assuming every millet seed product has the same status.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: No cited source evaluates proso millet in hydroponics.

height.reason: No home-scale cultivar dimensions are provided.

spacing.reason: Farm seeding rates are not household spacing.

light.reason: No indoor light requirement is established.

name: Adzuki Bean
summary: A warm-season annual pulse grown mainly for dry seed; tender pods may also be harvested green. Cultivated adzuki forms vary, and this species-level profile assigns no cultivar or compact-system fit.

identity.guidance: POWO accepts Vigna angularis. Adzuki/azuki is distinct from Vigna radiata (mung bean) and Phaseolus vulgaris (common bean). No cultivar or seed color is assigned.

growth.short: Annual, indeterminate crop; cultivated forms vary; field sources report 12–30 in tall
growth.guidance: The University of Wisconsin describes an indeterminate growth habit and reports 18–25 in (46–64 cm); Oregon State Extension reports 12–30 in (30–76 cm). Both are field-crop references, and UW notes erect versus branching/vining cultivated forms. This broad species record does not identify a cultivar or promise a container-grown size or a single habit. UF/IFAS's Florida home-garden guide describes plants as usually erect at 1–2 ft (30–61 cm), while noting that some gardeners report indeterminate growth. This reinforces variation among cultivated forms; no habit is assigned to an unidentified seed selection.

cultivation.short: Warm-season crop; steady soil moisture, drainage and frost protection matter
cultivation.guidance: Oregon State Extension gives 64–73°F (18–23°C) as an optimum growth range in its Columbia Basin production guide, notes frost sensitivity, and says soil moisture should be kept consistent although the crop is fairly drought resistant. It describes loamy, uncompacted soil; compaction and poor drainage are not suitable extrapolations to a container recipe. These are field-production conditions, not indoor or hydroponic specifications. UF/IFAS's Florida home-garden guide describes bean-like care without a trellis in its context, notes that cool nights favor production and that plants do not tolerate frost. Wisconsin documents erect and branching/vining forms in other production contexts, so trellis need is not universal. Florida dates and row spacing are not converted into a container or pod recommendation.

propagation.short: Seed-grown pulse; field emergence guidance only
propagation.guidance: Adzuki is established from seed. The cited field source reports emergence timing that varies with soil warmth; it does not document a home tray protocol or a cultivar-specific germination temperature.

harvest.short: Pods mature unevenly and can shatter; use pod and seed cues, not a fixed calendar
harvest.guidance: UW and Oregon State field guidance describe mixed pod maturity on indeterminate plants. For dry seed, Oregon State identifies yellow pods and hard seeds that rattle as harvest cues and warns that pods shatter readily; its 118-day figure is regional, not a household promise. The sources describe field harvest methods, not a home-tool procedure. UF/IFAS also documents harvesting tender young pods as snap beans about every 5–6 days in its Florida home-garden guide; that is a regional observation, not a universal schedule or a substitute for dry-seed harvest.

harvestUse.short: Dry mature seeds are used in savory dishes and sweet bean preparations
harvestUse.guidance: Oregon State Extension documents adzuki paste for pastries and desserts, as well as cooked beans in soups or rice and use as flour. The profile does not assign a seed color, named cultivar or regional harvest calendar to an unspecified seed selection.

care.short: Early weeds can outcompete slow-starting adzuki
care.guidance: University of Wisconsin describes adzuki as a poor weed competitor during its slow early growth and discusses mechanical cultivation in field rows after the primary leaves develop. Garden adaptation: once plants are established, check the bed or container for competing weeds and remove them carefully without disturbing the crop. Field-row timing is not a container schedule; no herbicide recommendation is carried over.

problems.short: Field reports include root rot, white mold and bacterial stem disease; symptoms are not detailed
problems.guidance: Oregon State Extension identifies root rot, white mold and bacterial stem disease in production fields. It associates root-rot risk with stressors including compaction and poor drainage, and describes rotation and disease-free seed as field-level prevention. The source does not provide a home-garden diagnosis or treatment threshold, so this is a watch-list rather than a visual diagnosis or pesticide recommendation.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: Field pulse guidance does not establish hydroponic production suitability.

growthHabits.reason: Species sources describe indeterminate growth with erect and branching/vining cultivated forms; this identity does not resolve which form the seed selection represents.

evidence.note: University of Wisconsin reports 18–25 in and Oregon State Extension 12–30 in in field-production contexts; UF/IFAS describes 1–2 ft in its Florida home-garden guide. This cross-context outer range is species-level, not cultivar-specific or a container prediction.

spread.reason: The sources do not establish a comparable species-level spread or home-garden footprint.

spacing.reason: Field crop row spacing is not a home-garden or pod-spacing recommendation.

light.reason: No indoor grow-light requirement is established.

name: Pigeon Pea
summary: A warm-climate, branching legume grown for green vegetable pods or mature dry seed. Growth duration and stature vary widely by type, photoperiod and region; this is not a dwarf or container cultivar.

identity.guidance: POWO accepts Cajanus cajan. Common names include pigeon pea, gandul and guandú; no regional landrace or cultivar is specified.

growth.short: Warm-climate shrub-like legume; stature and duration vary by type
growth.guidance: USDA NRCS describes Cajanus cajan as a warm-climate crop that may be long-lived and shrub-like. ICRISAT emphasizes strong type and environment variation; its backyard vegetable-pigeonpea examples were maintained for 3–4 years and exceeded 3 m, which is useful space context but not a universal size for this unspecified identity.

cultivation.guidance: USDA NRCS describes this as a warm-season crop. ICRISAT states vegetable pigeonpea is sensitive to photoperiod and temperature and cannot withstand waterlogging in its production guidance. These are crop/region-level outdoor references; no compact-system or hydroponic suitability is established.

propagation.short: Seed-grown crop; see the separate Seed Profile for establishment
propagation.guidance: USDA NRCS documents pigeonpea as a seed-grown crop. The separate Seed Profile carries seed-to-established-plant instructions; this Plant Profile does not repeat that protocol or the agricultural nursery method.

harvestUse.short: Use green pods as a vegetable or fully cooked mature seed
harvestUse.guidance: USDA NRCS says pigeonpea is eaten green as a vegetable or harvested dry as a pulse, and warns not to consume unprocessed seed because it contains tannin and trypsin inhibitors; it notes cooking removes trypsin inhibitors. ICRISAT describes immature pods for household vegetable use. This profile does not provide a complete food-preparation or preservation protocol.

care.short: Watch for weed competition during slow early growth
care.guidance: ICRISAT reports that young pigeonpea grows slowly and can face weed competition during roughly its first six weeks in field production. This supports monitoring competition while plants establish, not a universal home-garden weeding schedule; the publication's herbicide recommendations are not transferred.

flowering.short: Flowering responds to short days and local conditions
flowering.guidance: ICRISAT says pigeonpea phenology is sensitive to photoperiod and temperature and describes backyard plants beginning to flower as short days start. Under the publication's normal-moisture context, flowers and pods at several stages may occur on the same plant. This is not a fixed calendar date or a cultivar-specific response.

harvest.short: Green pods can be picked repeatedly; dry-seed harvest is a different endpoint
harvest.guidance: For household vegetable pigeonpea, ICRISAT describes picking immature pods as needed. USDA NRCS distinguishes green vegetable use from pulse crops harvested for dry seed; Texas A&M's roughly 140-day field estimate is not assigned to this unspecified type or a home-garden promise. No universal pod size, date or repeat interval is set.

problems.short: Monitor drainage and pod-level pest or disease signs
problems.guidance: ICRISAT identifies Fusarium wilt and sterility mosaic as important diseases in vegetable-pigeonpea production, and lists pod borers, pod fly and blister beetles among crop pests. This is a production-level watch list, not a symptom-based diagnosis or treatment schedule; the publication's older pesticide directions are intentionally excluded.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: Agricultural soil and forage guidance does not establish hydroponic suitability.

evidence.note: Species can develop a woody shrub habit; stature depends on cultivar and climate.

height.reason: No cultivar or regional mature height is specified.

spread.reason: No cultivar or regional mature spread is specified.

spacing.reason: Field plant spacing is not container or pod spacing.

light.reason: No indoor grow-light requirement is documented.

name: French Sorrel
summary: A low, spreading perennial herb grown for tart leaves. The common name sorrel is used for multiple taxa; this profile is specifically Rumex scutatus.

identity.guidance: POWO accepts Rumex scutatus. It is not Oxalis and should not be confused with field sorrel or other Rumex species sold under broad common names.

growth.short: Low, mound-forming perennial with a spreading habit
growth.guidance: Kew and Illinois Extension describe the species as perennial; NC State's narrative also calls it a creeping perennial. NC State's structured trait table separately labels it annual, so that internal conflict is retained. Illinois describes a mound/rosette with leaves 15–30 cm long; NC State gives a regional mature range of about 46–61 cm high and 41–91 cm wide. These are species-level garden references, not cultivar or container guarantees.

cultivation.short: Outdoor herb for sunny sites and suitable soil moisture
cultivation.guidance: Illinois Extension recommends full sun and rich, moist soil. NC State describes average, medium-moisture, well-drained soil and gives a regional full-sun to partial-shade range in its structured traits. These are outdoor references; neither establishes hydroponic suitability or indoor-light requirements.

propagation.short: Seed and division are documented; no seed-starting protocol is asserted here
propagation.guidance: Illinois Extension describes spring garden sowing and division every 3–4 years; NC State lists seed propagation. This established-plant profile records propagation routes only. Seed-starting details belong in a separately supported Seed Profile when available.

harvestUse.short: Tart leaves are used fresh or in cooked dishes
harvestUse.guidance: Illinois Extension lists mixed salads, sauces, soups, cheese dishes, and pork and fish dishes; it says sorrel is best fresh, though leaves freeze well. Its page notes acidity may discolor some metallic cookware. Leaves contain oxalic acid, which the source flags for people with certain health conditions; this is a source caution, not personalized medical advice.

problems.short: Regional sources report no known pests, but this is not a guarantee
problems.guidance: NC State reports no known insect pests or diseases in its regional plant profile. Treat that as a limited report, not proof that problems cannot occur. Illinois Extension also flags the leaves' oxalic-acid content as a dietary caution for some health conditions; it does not provide individualized health guidance.

harvest.short: Pick leaves as needed through the growing season
harvest.guidance: Illinois Extension says leaves may be harvested as needed through the season; very early leaves can have little flavor and develop their characteristic acidity as the season progresses. NC State separately notes leaves may become bitter later in the season. Neither source gives a universal starting size, interval or date, so none is assigned.

care.short: Remove seed stalks to protect usable leaf production
care.guidance: Illinois Extension says to remove seed stalks when they appear because they reduce the quantity of usable-quality leaves. It also recommends dividing plants every 3–4 years to maintain vigor. NC State likewise advises removing flowers promptly to promote leaf growth. These are outdoor source recommendations, not a guaranteed schedule for every climate or container.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: The cited sources describe outdoor soil cultivation and do not assess hydroponic production.

evidence.note: NC State describes a clumping/creeping habit; Illinois describes a mound and rosette.

spacing.reason: No exact garden spacing is assigned; mature spread is not converted into a planting interval.

light.reason: Outdoor sun exposure is documented, but this field represents indoor grow-light intensity; no conversion is made.

name: Cardoon
summary: A large thistle-like edible crop grown chiefly for blanched leaf stalks. It shares a species with globe artichoke horticultural forms; this record is cardoon and does not assert an artichoke cultivar.

identity.short: Cynara cardunculus; cardoon type, no named cultivar
identity.guidance: POWO accepts Cynara cardunculus. NC State describes cardoon and globe artichoke within the species complex; the edible harvested part and horticultural group distinguish this record from globe-artichoke profiles.

growth.short: Large, upright herbaceous perennial, sometimes grown as an annual
growth.guidance: NC State reports a broad regional size range of roughly 3–6 feet tall and 2–3 feet wide and describes deeply cut prickly foliage. These are outdoor regional dimensions, not container sizing.

cultivation.short: Full sun, moist well-drained soil; allow substantial space
cultivation.guidance: NC State recommends full sun and rich, moist but well-drained soil. The page also flags prickles, wind damage and potential naturalization; suitability depends on local climate and invasive status.

maintenance.short: Trim older leaves; protect the perennial root through winter where climate allows
maintenance.guidance: NC State says older leaves can be trimmed to keep the plant neat. In temperate locations it may persist as a perennial: foliage can die back in winter and regrow from a deep taproot; the source recommends heavy winter mulch in its regional context. It also reports summer dormancy in hot conditions. These are outdoor regional observations, not an indoor overwintering guarantee.

propagation.short: Seed and vegetative routes are documented
propagation.guidance: NC State lists seed, division and root cuttings. The cited page does not provide germination parameters; use seed-supplier instructions for sowing details, or a documented vegetative route when appropriate.

harvestUse.short: Blanch and cook the young leaf stalks
harvestUse.guidance: NC State identifies emerging leaf stalks as the principal vegetable harvest and says they are blanched, harvested and cooked. Do not substitute the edible flower-bud use of globe artichoke.

problems.short: Spines, wind damage and regional spread are relevant
problems.guidance: NC State reports prickly stems, possible wind damage, root rot, gray mold, powdery mildew, slugs and aphids; it warns cardoon can spread in some regions. Local invasive status matters.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: No hydroponic trial or system guidance is cited.

spacing.reason: The cited source's available-space category is not converted to exact spacing.

light.reason: Full-sun outdoor evidence is not mapped to indoor grow-light requirement.

name: Horseradish
summary: A hardy perennial grown for its pungent root. Root cuttings establish the crop, while leftover fragments can resprout, so choose a contained site. In Minnesota guidance, deep moist soil and careful seasonal harvest support usable roots; indoor and hydroponic cultivation are not established.

identity.guidance: POWO accepts Armoracia rusticana. Horseradish is distinct from radish (Raphanus sativus); the edible root is its principal horticultural product.

growth.short: Hardy perennial with large leaves and deep, spreading roots
growth.guidance: UMN Extension describes horseradish as a hardy, large-leaved perennial. NC State reports roughly 2–5 feet tall and 2–4 feet wide in its regional profile. Root fragments can resprout, so those outdoor dimensions do not define a contained footprint.

cultivation.short: UMN Minnesota guide: full sun and deep, rich, moist soil
cultivation.guidance: UMN Extension recommends a sunny site with deep, rich, moist loam; hard, shallow or stony soil can produce malformed roots and lower yields. Its soil preparation and row spacing are Minnesota garden guidance, not hydroponic parameters or pod spacing. No indoor light, EC or pH target is established.

care.short: Control weeds early; mulch helps conserve soil moisture
care.guidance: UMN Extension emphasizes weed control while plants are small and describes organic mulch as a way to retain soil moisture, keep soil cooler and suppress weeds. For growers seeking high-quality roots, its Minnesota production guide also describes lifting and stripping roots when the largest leaves are 8–10 inches long and repeating about six weeks later; this is an optional specialized practice, not a universal requirement.

propagation.short: Root cuttings or division are the documented routes
propagation.guidance: NC State lists root cuttings and division. UMN recommends planting root cuttings in early spring once soil is workable; its one-foot spacing and two-to-three-inch cover are soil-row instructions and must not be treated as hydroponic pod spacing. The selected sources do not establish a seed-starting protocol for this represented root-propagated crop.

harvest.short: In Minnesota, harvest in late fall before freeze or in spring
harvest.guidance: UMN's Minnesota guide delays fall harvest until late October or early November, just before the ground freezes, after late-summer and early-autumn root growth. It offers spring harvest as new growth begins when suitable cool storage is unavailable and notes roots left for two growing seasons may become stringy and woody. These are regional timing cues, not a universal calendar.

harvestUse.short: Use the edible root freshly grated as a pungent condiment
harvestUse.guidance: The edible product is the mature root. UW–Madison Extension describes freshly grating it and mixing with vinegar promptly because pungency changes after grating; see Harvest Use for the preparation and storage detail. No universal harvest age is assigned.

problems.short: Root fragments spread; flea beetles and root rot also matter
problems.guidance: NC State warns that root fragments can spread and resprout. UMN identifies flea beetles as a serious foliage pest and reports susceptibility to root rots; it recommends disease-free root cuttings and, in its Minnesota guidance, rotating the site rather than replanting horseradish there for three to four years. These are crop-level risks, not a claim that every plant will be affected.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: No source evaluates horseradish in hydroponics.

evidence.note: Perennial plant that can spread through root material.

spacing.reason: Soil-row spacing is not converted to indoor or hydroponic pod spacing.

light.reason: Outdoor full-sun guidance does not establish an indoor grow-light classification.

name: Prickly Pear Cactus
summary: A domesticated edible cactus grown for both young pads (nopales) and fruit (tuna). This species is distinguished from the many other Opuntia species also called prickly pear.

identity.guidance: POWO accepts Opuntia ficus-indica. Common names nopal, tuna and Indian fig cactus are used; generic prickly pear can refer to many Opuntia species, so this entry is taxonomically restricted.

growth.guidance: Kew describes a succulent shrub or tree; University of Arizona's campus arboretum describes the domesticated food plant and pad propagation. Mature form varies with cultivar and climate; no single dimensions are assigned.

cultivation.short: Warm, arid-adapted crop; use a well-drained site
cultivation.guidance: University of Arizona documents the edible cactus in arid-region cultivation and pad establishment. Its regional guidance should not be generalized to wet climates or used to infer indoor/hydroponic performance.

propagation.short: Rooted pads are the documented practical route
propagation.guidance: University of Arizona describes callusing a pad cutting before planting it shallowly in dry soil. This is vegetative propagation and preserves the selected plant; no seed-germination protocol is claimed.

harvestUse.short: Young pads are tender; fruit must be ripe and fully dethorned
harvestUse.guidance: University of Nevada Extension prefers younger pads for tenderness and says harvested fruit will not continue ripening, so fruit should be picked ripe. Both pads and fruit can carry glochids even when a plant is described as spineless; protective handling and complete removal are essential. The food-handling source discusses Opuntia broadly and does not establish that every Opuntia species is edible.

problems.short: Spines and glochids are a handling hazard; container spread needs control
problems.guidance: Extension sources emphasize careful handling of pads and fruit. No species-specific pest or disease profile is established here, and the record does not claim all Opuntia fruit is edible or palatable.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: No source evaluates this cactus in hydroponics.

evidence.note: Kew characterizes the species as a succulent shrub or tree.

height.reason: No cultivar- and climate-specific mature dimension is assigned.

spread.reason: No supported spread range is available for the represented plant.

spacing.reason: No exact garden spacing is provided; pad-planting instructions are not spacing guidance.

light.reason: Outdoor arid-culture context is not converted to indoor light intensity.
